Actually for OFT adapters, when you bridge FROM Ethereum to another chain, tokens get held in the adapter (or burned). When bridging TO Ethereum, the adapter releases tokens. So a release of 116,500 rsETH would correspond to an inbound bridge from another chain. But the adapter balance was 116,723.5 and fell to 223.5 — meaning the adapter released almost all of its held balance. Hmm, in LayerZero OFT pattern, the adapter holds tokens deposited by users bridging out; when bridging in, tokens are minted or released from... Actually for a non-mintable token like rsETH, the OFTAdapter locks/unlocks. Bridging in would unlock tokens from the adapter. So the adapter needs a float of tokens to release. A 116,500 release draining it to 223.5 could be legitimate if someone bridged 116,500 rsETH from another chain (e.g., someone had locked 116,500 on another chain earlier). But the timing and the subsequent behavior (fresh address receiving it, approving unlimited to Aave, supplying and borrowing max LTV, taking WETH out as ETH) strongly suggests an exploit: attacker drained the adapter via a forged/spoofed LayerZero delivery, then used the stolen rsETH as collateral on Aave to borrow WETH and extract value.

The risk is if rsETH price is wrong or rsETH becomes worthless (e.g., if the exploit means rsETH backing is broken, or if rsETH depegs).
